subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 41-year-old man with Crohn disease undergoes resection of the terminal ileum. Two months later he reports 6 to 8 large watery stools per day that persist even when he fasts and are not clearly related to meals. Colonoscopy shows no active inflammation, stool cultures are negative, and his vitamin A and vitamin D levels are low. Symptoms improve markedly when a bile acid binder is prescribed.
question: Which of the following best explains the chronic diarrhea in this patient?

options.text: Malabsorbed bile acids stimulate colonic water and electrolyte secretion
Unabsorbed long-chain fatty acids create an osmotic load in the colon
Loss of pancreatic lipase activity causes fat maldigestion
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth deconjugates bile acids
Reduced gastric acid secretion impairs protein digestion

explanation_correct: The terminal ileum is the only site of active bile acid reabsorption, so its resection interrupts the enterohepatic circulation and bile acids spill into the colon, where they stimulate colonic chloride and water secretion. This secretory diarrhea persists during fasting and responds to bile acid binders such as cholestyramine, and the loss of intraluminal bile acids also explains the low fat-soluble vitamin levels.

explanation_incorrect.B: Osmotic diarrhea from unabsorbed fatty acids would improve with fasting and would not respond so specifically to a bile acid binder.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pancreatic lipase deficiency would affect fat digestion but is not expected after limited ileal resection with an otherwise normal pancreas.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bacterial overgrowth produces a different pattern of diarrhea and is not the consequence of terminal ileal resection described here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Reduced gastric acid secretion does not cause high-volume secretory diarrhea or fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

educationalObjective: Terminal ileal resection causes bile acid diarrhea because malabsorbed bile acids stimulate colonic water and electrolyte secretion.
